title: Three days in the river
hook: he walks into the river Bein to bathe and is not seen for three days

segments.voice: Yesterday: the modikhana, the storehouse where the counting stopped at thirteen. Your line was tera, tera, all yours. What did you hand over with open hands? Day twenty-eight, the end of the week.

Before dawn in Sultanpur. The storekeeper does what he does every morning: he walks down to the small river at the edge of town, the Bein, to bathe before the day begins. A servant waits on the bank with his clothes. Nanak steps into the water, and goes under. And doesn't come up. The servant waits. Then shouts. Then runs for help. People come with ropes and nets. The governor himself, the story says, has the river searched. Nothing. No body, no clothes, no trace. By evening the town has decided: the storekeeper has drowned. His sister grieves. A day passes. Then another. Today, three days in the river.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, THE RIVER BEIN.` → `HE GOES UNDER.` → `AND DOESN'T COME UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the first thing to say plainly. Nobody knows what happened in those three days. No hymn of Nanak's narrates those three days. What we have is what the janamsakhis tell, and Sikhs treasure it. They say he was taken into the presence of God. There, he was given a cup of amrit, the nectar of immortality, and he drank it. And he was sent back with a charge: go into the world, remember the name, and teach others to remember it. After three days, on the third morning, he walked out of the river. Some tellings link this moment with the root verse you learned on days five and six; not every telling does. Sikh tradition remembers the river as the place Nanak's mission began. What it was like from the inside, the sources leave in the water. And look at the week that led here. A baby born in Talwandi. A sister who saw first. A boy asking what the letters meant. A cobra's shade. A true bargain. A storekeeper saying tera. All of it building, quietly, until one morning he walked into a river and came out someone the whole town would have to reckon with. Today a gurdwara called Ber Sahib stands on the riverbank. Tradition says the jujube tree there, the ber, is the one Nanak sat under.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT HAPPENED INSIDE.` · `A CUP OF AMRIT, AND A CHARGE.` · `WHERE THE MISSION BEGAN.` · `A WEEK THAT BUILT TO THIS.` · then, large: `SOME COME BACK CHANGED.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit by running water: a stream, a fountain, or just turn on a tap to a thin, steady trickle and sit beside it. Listen. Let the sound fill the room. Think of a time you went into something, a hard season, a trip, a loss, and came out different. You don't have to understand what happened. Just let the water run, and let yourself be changed a little by listening. The bell holds the time.
Three days in the river. Nanak disappears into the Bein at Sultanpur, and comes back, the stories say, with a mission.
screen: `THREE DAYS IN THE RIVER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: some come back changed. Today, go easy on someone who's come back from something different: a new parent, a grieving friend, a traveler. Tomorrow: what he said when he came out. Day twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Bein river as the place where Guru Nanak's mission began; pilgrims visit Gurdwara Ber Sahib in Sultanpur Lodhi and some bathe in the river.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: Vein, the river usually written Bein in English, at Sultanpur Lodhi.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nanak nearly drowned.
what it means: three days in which, the stories say, he was taken into God's presence and sent back to teach the name.
what a scholar hears: the janamsakhis differ on the details; the Puratan tradition tells of the cup of amrit and the charge. Nanak's own hymns don't narrate the three days.
